title: Creole and Cajun
intro: The roux, the trinity and the great pots of south Louisiana, and where the city's Creole cooking parts from the Cajun cooking of the country. Gumbo, étouffée and jambalaya are the lessons.

entries.title: Creole and Cajun
entries.summary: Creole cooking is the city's: New Orleans households and restaurants, French technique with butter, cream and tomato. Cajun cooking is the country's: the Acadians' descendants on the bayous and prairies, with smoked meats, dark roux and rice.
entries.guest: Creole is the city, Cajun the country: Creole means butter, cream and tomato, Cajun smoked meats and dark roux. Our menu is the city with country seasoning.

paras: Creole and Cajun are the two great cooking traditions of south Louisiana, and guests mix them up every week. Put simply, Creole belongs to the city and Cajun to the country. Creole is the cooking of New Orleans households and restaurants: French in technique, and shaped by the Spanish, West African, Caribbean, German and Italian cooks who worked in the city's kitchens. It leans on butter, cream and tomato, and on sauces made apart from the pot.

Cajun is the country food of the Acadians' descendants on the bayous and prairies west of the city: thrifty, one-pot cooking of smoked meats such as andouille and tasso, a roux, flour cooked in fat, taken dark, rice with nearly everything, and the game, fish and crawfish of the swamps and fields.

Creole cooking grew up in colonial New Orleans under French and then Spanish rule, in kitchens where cooks of African descent, enslaved and free, did much of the work. How those hands built it is the subject of the entry on Creole roots.

The Cajun story begins far to the north, in Acadia, today's Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in Maritime Canada. From 1755 the British expelled its French settlers, an exile Acadians call le Grand Dérangement, the great upheaval. Exiles reached Louisiana from the 1760s, among them a party led by Joseph Broussard that settled in the Bayou Teche country in 1765, and some three thousand came in all. In south Louisiana speech, Acadien wore down to Cadien and then, in English, to Cajun. Their cooking fed farmers, trappers and fishermen: one pot, a long simmer and whatever the land gave.

For the rest of the country, the two blurred in the 1980s. Paul Prudhomme, a Cajun-born chef who had cooked in New Orleans kitchens, grew famous with his French Quarter restaurant, K-Paul's, and his blackened redfish. Cajun became the national word for any spicy Louisiana food, and menus far from the bayous sold Cajun chicken and Cajun pasta. Many New Orleans cooks still wince when a Creole dish is called Cajun. His own story belongs to his entry.

The two traditions share far more than they divide: the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, the roux, gumbo, and rice under almost everything. Both grew from French cooking, and both took in African, Spanish and Native American ingredients and hands. The textbook line says a Creole gumbo carries tomato and seafood while a Cajun gumbo carries a darker roux, poultry and smoked sausage, and that a red jambalaya is Creole while a brown one is Cajun. Real kitchens cross the line every day: city cooks reach for andouille and tasso, and country cooks make tomato gravies. Teach the line, then expect it to blur.

Brennan's is a Creole house that borrows Cajun pantry staples: tasso, andouille and rice dressing. Andouille, a coarse smoked pork sausage, gives the Seafood Gumbo its smoky backbone. Tasso, a spiced and smoked seasoning meat cut from the pork shoulder, seasons the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. The South Louisiana Rice Dressing, rice folded with browned meat and the trinity, is country cooking among the dinner sides; the menu prints no description, so confirm its meats with the kitchen.

When a guest asks the difference, give the one-line answer and go back to the menu: Creole is the city, Cajun the country, and our menu is the city with country seasoning. If they want more, add one sentence: Creole cooking is French technique with butter, cream and tomato, and Cajun cooking is the Acadians' country food of smoked meats, dark roux and rice. Never call the whole menu Cajun.

Say the word Creole with care. It comes from the Spanish criollo, born in the colony, and in Louisiana it was used by people of many backgrounds born there: descendants of French and Spanish settlers, free people of colour, Africans and their descendants, and families of mixed ancestry. In the century after the Civil War the word was fought over, and who may call themselves Creole is still argued. Use it of the food and the city's tradition, and let guests describe themselves.

entries.title: The holy trinity and the mirepoix
entries.summary: Onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and softened together at the start of a Creole or Cajun dish. It is south Louisiana's answer to the French mirepoix, with green pepper standing where the carrot would be.
entries.guest: The holy trinity is onion, celery and green pepper cooked together. It is the base of our gumbo, the turtle soup and the Creole sauce on the shrimp and grits.

paras: The holy trinity is the aromatic base of south Louisiana cooking: onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and cooked together in fat until soft. It plays the part that mirepoix plays in a French kitchen, and the difference is the point. Where mirepoix takes carrot, the trinity takes green pepper, which gives a sharper, greener savour and less of the carrot's sugar.

It is shared by both of Louisiana's great cooking traditions. Creole cooking, the city cooking of New Orleans, puts it under tomato, butter and stock; Cajun cooking, from the prairies and bayous to the west, puts it into dark roux, game and smoked meat.

Mirepoix itself is classically two parts onion to one part each of carrot and celery, by weight, cut small for a sauce and large for a long-simmered stock. A white mirepoix leaves out the carrot, often taking leek in its place, so that a pale stock or sauce stays pale. A matignon is a mirepoix cooked gently in butter, often with ham, and left in the dish to be eaten rather than strained out. Spain's sofrito and Italy's soffritto are cousins further off.

The vegetables are old in Louisiana kitchens; the name is newer. It nods to the Catholic faith of south Louisiana and was most likely popularised by the chef Paul Prudhomme in the 1980s. Garlic is added so often that some cooks call it the pope.

Why pepper for carrot? Nobody has documented it. The usual telling credits the hot climate and the Spanish taste for peppers, but an LSU AgCenter horticulturist points out that both crops do well in Louisiana, carrots in the cool season and peppers in the warm, so treat it as a story rather than a fact. Either way the result is plain in the pot: a sharper, more savoury base that suits smoked meat, seafood and dark roux.

Ratios vary by cook, and the argument is an old one. Many use equal parts of all three; others follow the mirepoix habit of two parts onion to one part each of celery and pepper, which gives a rounder, sweeter base. For a pot of gumbo for eight, about 300 g (10.5 oz) of diced onion to 150 g (about 5 oz) each of celery and green pepper is a sound start. In a professional kitchen, the chef's recipe settles it.

Cut the three to the same small dice so they soften together; the cuts themselves are taught under knife cuts. In a gumbo or an étouffée the trinity goes straight into the hot roux, which all but stops the roux darkening, give or take a shade, and cooks the vegetables in its heat; stir hard, because the pot will hiss and steam. For a Creole sauce it is sweated instead: cooked in butter or oil over moderate heat until soft and translucent, ten minutes or so, without browning, before the garlic and then the tomatoes and stock go in.

Garlic follows once the trinity has softened, for a minute or two, because it scorches faster than the others and turns bitter when it does. At the end, sliced green onion, the spring onion of a British market, and chopped flat-leaf parsley are stirred in or scattered over the bowl. They are the finishing herbs of Louisiana cooking, fresh and green against the long-cooked base.

At Brennan's the trinity is in the Seafood Gumbo, the Turtle Soup, the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing. It is the reason those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.

At the table the trinity needs only a sentence: onion, celery and green bell pepper, cooked together as the base of Creole and Cajun cooking. Say holy trinity as it reads. A guest who avoids onion, celery or peppers should hear that the trinity is in the base of the gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce and the rice dressing, and the question goes to the kitchen before the order is fired.

entries.title: The roux ladder
entries.summary: The Louisiana roux ladder runs from white and blond through peanut butter and milk chocolate to dark chocolate, or brick. Each rung takes longer, tastes deeper and thickens less, and each dish wants its own rung.
entries.guest: A roux is flour cooked in fat until it toasts; the darker it goes, the deeper the flavour. It is part of why a gumbo tastes deep rather than brothy.

paras: A roux, said ROO, is flour cooked in fat and stirred until it reaches the colour the dish needs. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel, the milk sauce, and velouté, the stock sauce, and brown for espagnole, the brown sauce, though Escoffier's brown roux stops at a light, nutty brown; the French roux have their own entry. Louisiana cooks keep going, naming the stages by familiar colours: white, blond, peanut butter, milk chocolate, which is a medium brown, and dark chocolate, also called brick. Each rung up takes longer, smells and tastes deeper, and thickens less.
The colour of the roux is the flavour of the pot: pulled too early, the dish tastes flat; taken too far, it tastes burnt.

Use a heavy pot over a medium flame. For a dark roux use oil or lard, not whole butter: its milk solids scorch long before the flour turns brown, so whole butter is kept for the pale rungs. Clarified butter, its milk solids taken out, can go darker, as in the classical French brown roux. Weigh equal amounts of fat and flour, such as 225 g (8 oz) of each. Heat the fat until it shimmers, whisk in the flour, then work with a flat-ended wooden spoon that reaches the corners, and never stop stirring.

Rough times over a medium flame: blond in 5 to 10 minutes, peanut butter in 15 to 20, milk chocolate in 25 to 35, and dark chocolate in 40 minutes or more. Read the roux, not the clock. As it darkens it loosens and runs more freely, and its smell moves from raw flour to toast, roasted nuts, then cocoa and coffee. The oven roux is the slower, gentler path: bake the fat and flour uncovered at 175°C (350°F), stirring every 20 to 30 minutes, for 1.5 to 2.5 hours.

A roux keeps cooking in its own heat, so stop it just before the colour you want. In Louisiana the trinity does the stopping: the cool, wet onion, celery and pepper go in all at once, drop the temperature and halt the browning while the roux softens them. The stock follows, whisked in gradually.

Darker means more flavour and less thickening, and the reason is the starch. Flour is mostly starch, long chains of glucose packed into granules. In a pale roux the granules are barely changed, and when liquid goes in they swell and thicken it. Long heat breaks those chains into shorter ones called dextrins, which brown and taste toasty but can no longer swell and bind. Flour for flour, a dark roux thickens far less than a blond one, so a gumbo, though far thinner than a sauce, takes about as much flour as a medium béchamel: around 50 g (1.75 oz) a litre.

Each rung has its dishes. White and blond thicken most French sauces, and a brown roux the classical espagnole; blond to peanut butter suits an étouffée, which wants body and a buttery colour. Milk chocolate suits the gravy of grillades, a Creole courtbouillon and a Creole turtle soup. Dark chocolate belongs to chicken and andouille gumbo, duck and sausage gumbo, sauce piquante and most New Orleans seafood gumbos, the published Brennan's recipe among them, though some cooks stop a seafood gumbo a shade lighter so the shrimp and crab stay in front. In a professional kitchen the chef sets how dark each house roux goes, because the colour sets both the flavour and how much flour the recipe needs.

Black flecks or a sharp, acrid smell mean the roux has burnt, and there is no rescue: the bitterness runs through the whole pot, so start again. Hot roux also burns cooks. A dark roux runs well over 150°C (302°F) and clings to skin like hot sugar, which is why Louisiana cooks call it Cajun napalm. Wear long sleeves, keep water away from the pot, never taste from the spoon, and add the spitting trinity away from your face.

At Brennan's, roux is part of why the Seafood Gumbo and the Turtle Soup taste deep rather than brothy. Both stand on a well-browned roux, and the house's published gumbo recipe, as the lineup notes give it, starts with a dark mahogany roux, but how dark the kitchen takes each one is the chef's call: confirm it at lineup before describing it. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Gumbo
entries.summary: Gumbo is Louisiana's soup-stew, served over rice and thickened with roux, okra, filé or a mix of them. Its name most likely comes from a Bantu word for okra, and its pot holds the state's history.
entries.guest: Gumbo is Louisiana's great soup-stew, built on a roux and served over rice. Ours is seafood: shrimp, crab, oysters and smoky andouille over popcorn rice.

paras: Gumbo is a Louisiana soup-stew served over rice. It is thicker than a soup and thinner than a stew or a gravy, and it is thickened by roux, which is flour cooked in fat until it toasts, by okra, by filé, which is ground dried sassafras leaves, or by a mix of them. Nearly every modern gumbo starts with a roux and the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, then stock, a long simmer and whatever the cook has: seafood, chicken, sausage, duck or greens. It is the dish most guests come to Louisiana expecting, and often the first one they ask about.

Most gumbos follow one shape. Cook a roux in a heavy pot to the colour the recipe calls for, stir in the trinity to stop it, then the garlic. Add smoked sausage such as andouille, then whisk in hot stock gradually and bring it to a simmer. Simmer an hour or more, skimming the fat that rises and seasoning as it goes. Poultry goes in early enough to turn tender; seafood goes in only for the last few minutes, so it stays sweet. Finish with sliced green onion and parsley. How okra and filé go in is a lesson of its own.

Rice goes in the bowl, never in the pot: plain long-grain rice cooked apart, with the gumbo ladled around it. Cooked in the pot, the rice would drink the liquid and turn the gumbo to porridge. In some Cajun homes a scoop of potato salad goes alongside, or straight into the bowl.

Gumbos come in families. Seafood gumbo carries shrimp, crab and oysters in a stock made from their shells. Chicken and andouille is the everyday country gumbo: a dark roux, chicken and smoked sausage. Duck and sausage is the hunters' gumbo of duck season, its roux taken very dark. Gumbo z'herbes is the green gumbo of many greens, tied to Lent and Holy Thursday. Each has its own lesson.

The city and country line shows here too. Creole gumbos often carry tomato and seafood, and okra; Cajun gumbos lean to a dark roux, poultry and smoked sausage, and rarely see tomato. Like every line between Creole and Cajun, it blurs in real kitchens.

A gumbo tells Louisiana's history in one bowl. The name most likely comes from ki-ngombo, a word for okra in the Bantu languages of west-central Africa, shortened to gombo; okra itself crossed the Atlantic with the slave trade. The other theory traces the name to kombo, a Choctaw word for filé, and filé itself came from the Choctaw. The roux is French, taken darker in Louisiana, and Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks added their hands, the German settlers upriver among them with their smoked sausage. Written accounts place gumbo at a governor's reception in New Orleans in 1803, and Lafcadio Hearn's La Cuisine Créole of 1885 already printed several gumbos.

A burnt roux makes a bitter pot, and nothing rescues it. A thin, watery gumbo usually means a dark roux was asked to thicken more liquid than it could. A greasy surface means the fat was not skimmed. Rubbery shrimp and shrunken oysters went in too early or were reheated too hard, and mushy rice was cooked in the pot.

At Brennan's the gumbo is the Seafood Gumbo: shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice, a signature at both meals and the other soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast. Its own entry tells its story; anything in tonight's pot beyond what the menu prints is a lineup question.

Say GUM-boh, and describe it in a breath: Louisiana's soup-stew, built on a roux and served over rice. Tell the guest what is in tonight's bowl, then how it eats: rice and gumbo in the same spoon. Asked whether ours is spicy, the house answer is mild to moderate. Whether bread or hot sauce comes with it is the house's call, so learn it at lineup. If a guest asks about okra or filé, or about shellfish or flour, read the service note and ask the kitchen rather than guess.

faults.cause: The roux burnt before the trinity went in.
faults.fix: Start again; a burnt roux cannot be rescued, and it spoils every ingredient added after it.

faults.cause: Too much stock for the roux, often a dark roux, which thickens less.
faults.fix: Simmer it down, or stir in a little roux made in another pan.

faults.cause: Fat from the roux and the sausage was never skimmed.
faults.fix: Skim through the simmer, and lift the fat that rises before serving.

faults.cause: The seafood went in too early or was boiled on reheating.
faults.fix: Add seafood only for the last few minutes, and reheat gently.

faults.fault: Mushy rice and a porridge-thick pot
faults.cause: The rice was cooked in the gumbo.
faults.fix: Cook the rice apart and put it in the bowl.

brennans.how: Ours is the Seafood Gumbo: shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice, a Brennan's signature at both meals and the other soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.

entries.title: Roux, okra and filé
entries.summary: The three ways a Louisiana cook gives a gumbo its body: a roux of flour cooked in fat, okra cooked down until its sticky juice thickens the pot, and filé, ground sassafras leaves stirred in at the end.
entries.guest: Gumbo takes its body from a roux, from okra, from filé, which is ground sassafras leaves, or from a mix of them. I can ask the kitchen how tonight's is made.

paras: A gumbo is a soup that eats like a stew, and something has to give it that body. Louisiana cooks have three thickeners, and each brings flavour as well as texture. Roux is flour cooked in fat until it toasts. Okra is a green pod whose sticky juice thickens the pot as it simmers. Filé (FEE-lay) is the dried leaf of the sassafras tree, ground to a green powder and stirred in at the very end.

Nearly every modern gumbo starts on a roux, and many add okra or filé as well. The choice changes the bowl: roux gives toasty depth, okra a silky, faintly grassy body, filé an earthy, herbal note and a soft, velvety thickness.

Roux comes first. Cook oil and an equal weight of flour in a heavy pot, stirring without stopping, to the colour the dish wants, usually a deep brown for gumbo. The trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, goes straight into the hot roux: it cools the pot, stops the browning and softens in the fat. Stock follows a ladle at a time, whisked hard so no lumps form. Allow about 50 g (1.75 oz) of flour to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock: a generous measure for so thin a pot, because a dark roux thickens far less than a pale one, as the roux ladder explains.

Okra is sliced into rounds about 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick and smothered first: cooked down in a little oil over a medium heat, stirred often, for 20 to 30 minutes. At first it throws long, sticky strings, which cooks call the rope; this is its mucilage, a soluble fibre that thickens water. Cooking it down tames the rope, and a splash of tomato or vinegar helps. The okra then simmers in the gumbo for at least 30 minutes more, where what is left of its mucilage gives the pot body.

Filé goes in last, and never into a boiling pot. Take the gumbo off the heat and stir in 5 to 15 ml (1 to 3 tsp) for a pot for eight, or pass it at the table for a pinch a bowl. Boiled, filé turns a gumbo stringy and gluey, which is why many cooks add it bowl by bowl: the rest of the pot can then be reheated.

The old Creole households thickened with whatever the season gave. Okra is a summer crop, so summer brought okra gumbo, gombo févi in Creole French; sassafras leaves could be dried and pounded to keep, so the winter pot was a filé gumbo. Hence the old rule that okra and filé do not share a pot: they were the two halves of the year, and both thicken through a slippery mucilage, so together they can make a gumbo gluey. Many cooks break the rule today, Brennan's published recipe among them.

Thickening faults show at the spoon. A thin gumbo had too little roux for its colour, or okra that did not simmer long enough; a slimy one, okra that went in raw; a stringy, gluey one, filé that met the boil, which cannot be undone. A good gumbo coats a spoon lightly and still pours.

The Brennan's menu describes the Seafood Gumbo by its seafood, andouille and popcorn rice and names no thickener. The house's published recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux and carries okra, tomato and filé, but whether the dining room gumbo follows it is confirmed at lineup, so say published recipe, never menu. Okra is on the menu, but crisp: fried into chips on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits and worked into the tostada, where it thickens nothing.

Guests ask whether there is okra, whether it is thick and whether there is flour. Say what you know: a gumbo is usually built on a roux, and okra and filé are the other two thickeners. A guest who asks about flour or gluten goes straight to the kitchen, never to a guess. A guest who dislikes okra can be told that cooked down well it melts into the broth, and the kitchen can say whether it is in tonight's pot.

entries.title: Seafood gumbo
entries.summary: A New Orleans classic: Gulf shrimp, blue crab and oysters in a dark broth built on roux, the trinity and a stock of shells, often with tomato and smoked sausage, the seafood added last and served over rice.
entries.guest: Our Seafood Gumbo is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice: savoury, briny and gently smoky.

paras: Seafood gumbo is a New Orleans classic: a dark, brothy stew of Gulf shrimp, blue crab and oysters, built on a roux and the trinity and served over rice. It is Creole cooking at its most typical, a French roux, West African okra and the catch of the coast in one pot.

Its whole skill is timing. The base of roux, vegetables, stock and seasoning wants an hour or more to come together; the seafood wants minutes. A good seafood gumbo is built so the two meet at the last moment.

Make the stock first: shrimp shells and heads and cleaned blue crab bodies, simmered with onion trimmings, celery and bay for 20 to 30 minutes, then strained. In a heavy pot, cook oil and flour to a dark roux, stir in the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, and cook until soft before the garlic goes in for a minute. Sliced andouille or smoked sausage, browned first in many kitchens, brings smoke and depth.

Whisk in the hot stock a ladle at a time, about 3 litres (about 3 quarts) for a pot for eight, then add tomato if the cook uses it, with bay, thyme, cayenne and black pepper. In the Creole tradition, okra, smothered first, goes in now. Simmer gently for about an hour, skimming the oil that rises, until the broth coats a spoon lightly and the flavours have married.

The seafood goes in last, in order of how long it needs. Shrimp take 2 to 3 minutes, until they turn pink and curl. Picked crab claws and lump crabmeat, the large pieces of body meat, are sold cooked, so they are only warmed through. Oysters and their liquor, the briny juice from the shell, go in at the very end and are done as soon as their edges curl, a minute or so. Off the heat, check the salt; filé, for the cooks who use it, is stirred in now or passed at the table.

The faults come from heat and time. Rubbery shrimp and shrunken, leathery oysters mean the seafood cooked too long, usually because the whole pot was held hot after it went in. That is why some kitchens hold the base on its own and add the seafood to each batch, or even each order, so it meets the heat for minutes. Lump crab falls into threads if stirred hard; fold it in. A bitter, burnt taste means the roux scorched, and nothing hides it. Cooling and keeping a pot follow the kitchen's own rules.

Reheating follows the same rule. Bring a held base back to a gentle simmer before the seafood goes in. A pot reheated with its seafood already in is warmed slowly, stirred gently so the crab stays whole, and served as soon as it is hot, never brought to the boil.

The Brennan's Seafood Gumbo has its own entry; here it shows the method at work. The menu names shrimp, crab and oysters with andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice, and the house's published recipe adds the seafood at the very end so it stays tender. Whether the dining room follows that recipe is a lineup question.

Seafood gumbo is served in a bowl over a mound of rice, never cooked with the rice, and finished with sliced green onion (spring onion) and chopped parsley. Tell the guest what is in it in plain words: shrimp, crab, oysters and smoked sausage in a rich, savoury broth. Asked whether the Brennan's gumbo is spicy, the house answer is mild to moderate. Questions about shellfish, pork or how the gumbo is thickened go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Gumbo z'herbes
entries.summary: Green gumbo: an odd number of greens, collards, mustard, turnip tops, spinach and cabbage among them, cooked down and chopped or puréed. Once a meatless Lenten dish, it is now the rich Holy Thursday gumbo of New Orleans.
entries.guest: Gumbo z'herbes is green gumbo, many kinds of greens cooked down with smoked meats and served over rice, the traditional New Orleans dish for Holy Thursday.

paras: Gumbo z'herbes is green gumbo: a pot of many greens, collards, mustard greens, turnip tops, spinach, cabbage and more, simmered soft, then chopped fine or puréed and cooked on in their own liquor until the broth turns deep green. Where most gumbos are about seafood or poultry, this one is about the garden.
The name is New Orleans French. Gumbo aux herbes, gumbo with greens, runs together in speech so that the x of aux is sounded as a z on the front of herbes: z'herbes.

Wash the greens in several changes of cold water, lifting them out so the grit stays behind, and strip the tough stems. Simmer them in salted water or light stock, the sturdy collards first and the tender spinach last, until all are soft, 30 to 45 minutes. Lift them out, keep every drop of the cooking liquor, and chop the greens fine or purée them.

Brown the meats in the pot: smoked sausage, ham and fresh hot sausage are common, and some cooks add brisket or chicken. If the recipe uses a roux, make it in that fat, add onion and garlic, then return the greens with enough liquor for a thick, soupy stew. Season with thyme, bay and cayenne, and simmer for about an hour, stirring often, because puréed greens settle and catch on the bottom. Serve over rice.

Versions part on two questions. Roux or none: older pots often took their body from the puréed greens alone, while many modern cooks start on a roux. Meat or none: the Lenten pot was meatless, while the Holy Thursday pot carries smoked sausage, ham and more. Okra is rare; filé sometimes finishes it. Its cousins are the leafy green stews of West Africa and the Caribbean, such as callaloo, cooked with greens and often salted meat, crab or smoked fish, which makes the pot as much African as French, whatever its name.

In the old Catholic households of New Orleans, gumbo z'herbes was a Lenten dish, made without meat for Good Friday, when Catholics fasted and went without meat. In time it moved to Holy Thursday, the day before, and filled up with meat, a feast before the fast rather than the fast itself.

The pot that made the custom famous was Leah Chase's at Dooky Chase's Restaurant, made once a year for Holy Thursday. She insisted on an uneven number of greens, nine in her recipe, and the custom is told this way: each green stands for a new friend in the year ahead, and an odd number brings luck.

Grit in the bowl means the greens were not washed well enough. A harsh, bitter pot has too much mustard or turnip for its milder greens; balance it with cabbage or spinach and season well, since salt tames bitterness. A scorched taste means the thick purée sat on the heat unstirred.

Our gumbo is the seafood one, so gumbo z'herbes comes to the table as a question, most often in Lent. Describe it plainly: many greens cooked down, rich with smoked meats in its Holy Thursday form, served over rice. A guest who asks whether a gumbo z'herbes is vegetarian should hear that most modern versions carry meat, and that only the kitchen that made a pot can answer for it.

entries.title: Étouffée
entries.summary: Smothered: crawfish tails or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce of blond to peanut butter roux, the trinity and a little shell stock, spooned over rice. A sauce rather than a soup, and in its crawfish form a Cajun classic.
entries.guest: Étouffée means smothered: crawfish or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce with onion, celery and pepper, spooned over rice, with a gentle heat.

paras: Étouffée means smothered. Crawfish tails or shrimp are cooked in a thick, glossy sauce of butter, the trinity and a little stock, just enough to coat them, and the dish is spooned over rice. It is a sauce, not a soup: where a gumbo is ladled, an étouffée sits on the rice and holds its shape for a moment before it settles.
In its crawfish form it is a Cajun classic, built on the sweet tail meat and the golden fat of crawfish in their spring season.

Simmer the crawfish or shrimp shells in water with onion trimmings and bay for 20 to 30 minutes for a quick stock, and strain it. Crawfish tails are usually bought cooked and peeled, packed with their fat, so a crawfish étouffée often uses a light shrimp or seafood stock instead. Melt butter in a wide, heavy pan, about 115 g (4 oz) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails, stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and cook it to blond or peanut butter brown, 10 to 20 minutes over a medium heat. Add the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, soften it, then add the garlic.

Whisk in the stock a little at a time, only about 350 ml (about 1.5 cups) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails, so the sauce coats a spoon heavily. Season with cayenne, black pepper and salt and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes. Add the tails with their fat, or the shrimp, for 3 to 5 minutes, only until hot through or pink. Finish with sliced green onion and chopped parsley, and serve over white rice.

The yellow-orange crawfish fat is not true fat but the hepatopancreas, a fat-rich organ that digests the crawfish's food. It carries much of the flavour and colours the sauce gold, so a Cajun cook would never rinse it away.

Étouffée has two main lines. The Cajun crawfish étouffée of the Breaux Bridge country is blond to pale brown, buttery and usually made without tomato, its colour from the fat; Creole cooks in the city often add tomato, which reddens it and gives an acid edge. Some cooks make no roux at all and let butter, crawfish fat and reduced stock thicken it, a richer, looser sauce.

Know it against its neighbours. A gumbo is a soup, with a darker roux and far more liquid; an étouffée is a thick sauce on a lighter roux. A Cajun stew or fricassée goes the other way, a darker roux and a gravy loose enough to ladle, while an étouffée is smothered thick.

Breaux Bridge, in St. Martin Parish, holds the Cajun claim. The history 64 Parishes tells credits the Hébert sisters, Yolie and Marie, whose parents ran the town's Hébert Hotel in the 1920s, with an early version they called a crawfish courtbouillon, and Aline Guidry Champagne with the version that took the name. In the late 1940s she left out the tomato, garlic and celery, told guests in her kitchen she was smothering the crawfish, and the dish went on the Rendezvous Club menu in 1950. The legislature named Breaux Bridge the Crawfish Capital of the World in 1959.

Describe it plainly: crawfish tails, or shrimp, smothered in a thick butter sauce with onion, celery and pepper, over rice, with a gentle heat. Our menu carries no étouffée; the house's crawfish dish is the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost, and how their filling is made is not printed, so ask the kitchen before describing it. Questions about shellfish, butter or flour in any dish go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Jambalaya, red and brown
entries.summary: Rice cooked in one pot with meat, seafood or both, the grains drinking a seasoned stock until none is left. Red jambalaya, with tomato, belongs to the city; brown, coloured by well-browned meat and onions, belongs to the Cajun country.
entries.guest: Jambalaya is Louisiana rice cooked in one pot with sausage, chicken or shrimp, so every grain takes up the seasoned stock. Red has tomato; brown gets its colour from browned meat.

paras: Jambalaya is rice cooked in one pot with meat, seafood or both. The meat and the trinity go in first, then stock, then raw long-grain rice, and the lid goes on. The rice drinks the stock until none is left, so every grain carries the seasoning of the pot: not a base under a sauce but the dish itself.
It is the party and church-fair dish of south Louisiana: one pot feeds a crowd, and smoked sausage, chicken or shrimp season every grain of rice.

Red jambalaya, the Creole kind of New Orleans, carries tomato, which tints the rice a soft red and gives it a gentle acidity; shrimp with ham or sausage is a common pairing. Brown jambalaya, the Cajun kind of the country, has no tomato. Its colour comes from browning: chicken and pork or smoked sausage seared hard, onions cooked down deep brown, and the browned bits scraped up into the stock. A pale brown jambalaya means the browning was rushed.

Its kin cook rice in a seasoned liquid too: Spanish paella, with meat or seafood in a wide pan, and West African jollof, in a base of tomato, pepper and onion. The origin of the name is disputed: one account points to a Provençal word, jambalaia, another joins jambon, French for ham, to a West African word for rice, and none is proven.

For about eight: brown 450 g (1 lb) of sliced smoked sausage in a heavy pot, then 900 g (2 lb) of chicken thigh in pieces, in batches so it sears rather than steams, and lift them out. For a red jambalaya, soften 2 onions, 2 sticks of celery and 1 green pepper, diced, for 8 to 10 minutes, scraping up the browned bits. For a brown one, cook the onions alone first, stirring, until deep brown, 20 to 30 minutes, then add the celery and pepper. Add 4 cloves of garlic for the last minute. For a red jambalaya add 400 g (14 oz) of chopped tomatoes. Return the meat and season with cayenne, thyme, bay, salt and pepper.

Add the stock, bring it to a full boil and taste it: it should be a little saltier and hotter than seems right, because the rice takes up every drop. Allow 1 part long-grain rice to about 1.5 to 2 parts liquid by volume in all: 480 ml (2 cups) of rice to 720 to 960 ml (3 to 4 cups) of liquid, the lower figure when the vegetables are wet, more for parboiled rice. In a red jambalaya the 400 g (14 oz) of tomatoes count as about 300 ml (1.25 cups) of that liquid, so use that much less stock.

Stir the rice in once, return it to the boil, cover, turn the heat to its lowest and leave it for 20 to 25 minutes, then rest it covered off the heat for 10 minutes; the chicken will be well past 74°C (165°F). Never stir under the lid: stirring breaks the grains and rubs off starch that turns the pot to mush. In the great outdoor pots, cast-iron kettles over gas flames that feed hundreds, cooks turn the rice once or twice from the bottom with a paddle so the top cooks evenly: a gentle turn, not a stir.

Mushy rice comes from stirring or too much liquid, often the tomato's juice left uncounted. A scorched bottom means heat too high under a thin pot; never scrape the burnt layer into the rest. Crunchy grains on top mean steam escaped: add a little hot stock, cover tightly and give it 5 minutes more. Bland rice means the stock was under-seasoned, and salt stirred in later never reaches the centre of the grain.

Gonzales, in Ascension Parish, calls itself the Jambalaya Capital of the World, a title Governor John McKeithen proclaimed in 1968, the year of its first Jambalaya Festival, which still gathers cooks and their great pots each spring.

Jambalaya is not on our printed menus, but guests ask, and the answer is short: Louisiana rice cooked in one pot with sausage, chicken or shrimp, red with tomato in the city, brown without it in the country. Cooked rice left warm is a known risk, because the spores of Bacillus cereus, a bacterium common on rice, survive cooking, so kitchens hold it at 57°C (135°F) or above or cool it fast. Questions about pork, shellfish or spice in any dish go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What is a jambalaya?
cards.back: Long-grain rice cooked in one pot with meat, seafood or both, the grains drinking the seasoned stock until none is left.

cards.front: What separates a red jambalaya from a brown one?
cards.back: Red, the Creole city kind, carries tomato; brown, the Cajun country kind, has none and takes its colour from well-browned meat and onions.

cards.front: Where does a brown jambalaya get its colour?
cards.back: From browning: meat seared hard in the pot, onions cooked down deep brown, and the browned bits scraped up into the stock.

cards.front: What is the working ratio of rice to liquid in a jambalaya?
cards.back: About 1 part long-grain rice to 1.5 to 2 parts liquid by volume, counting tomato juice, with more for a parboiled rice.

cards.front: Why is a jambalaya never stirred once the lid is on?
cards.back: Stirring breaks the grains and rubs starch from them, which turns the pot to mush; the rice is left covered on the lowest heat.

cards.front: How long does the rice cook, and how is it finished?
cards.back: Covered on the lowest heat for 20 to 25 minutes, then rested off the heat, lid still on, for 10 minutes before fluffing.

cards.front: Why taste and season the stock before the rice goes in?
cards.back: The rice takes up every drop, so the stock should taste slightly over-seasoned; salt added afterwards never reaches the centre of the grain.

cards.front: Which town calls itself the Jambalaya Capital of the World?
cards.back: Gonzales, in Ascension Parish, proclaimed so by Governor John McKeithen in 1968, the year of its first Jambalaya Festival.

cards.front: Which rice dishes are kin to jambalaya?
cards.back: Spanish paella and West African jollof: each cooks rice in one pan or pot in a seasoned liquid, with meat, seafood or tomato.

cards.front: Where does the word jambalaya come from?
cards.back: Nobody knows for certain: one account points to a Provençal word, jambalaia; another joins jambon, ham, to a West African word for rice.

cards.front: What scorches the bottom of a jambalaya, and how do you prevent it?
cards.back: Heat too high under a thin pot, or too little liquid; use a heavy pot on the lowest flame and never scrape burnt rice into the rest.

entries.title: Creole courtbouillon
entries.summary: Redfish cooked gently in a thick, rust-red gravy of roux, tomato and the trinity, with garlic, bay, lemon and wine, and served over rice. Said coo-bee-YON in Louisiana, it borrows a French word and means a different dish.
entries.guest: Courtbouillon, said coo-bee-YON here, is redfish simmered in a rich tomato and roux gravy with onion, celery, pepper and a little wine, spooned over rice.

paras: A Creole courtbouillon is fish, most often redfish, cooked gently in a thick tomato gravy built on a roux and the trinity, seasoned with garlic, bay, thyme, lemon and red or white wine, and in some recipes allspice. It is served over rice, the fish in thick slices or bone-in steaks, or whole when the cook wants a show.

The name trips people up. In the French kitchen a court-bouillon is a short, quick broth of water, wine or vinegar and aromatics for poaching fish, thin and clear, and it has its own entry. In Louisiana the same word, run together and said coo-bee-YON, means this thick, red, saucy dish. A cook who knows both will never confuse an order.

For about six: cut 1.4 kg (3 lb) of redfish fillet into thick pieces, season them with salt and cayenne and keep them cold. In a wide, heavy pot make a roux of 60 g (2 oz) each of oil and flour, cooked to peanut butter or milk chocolate brown, 15 to 30 minutes over a medium flame. Add 2 onions, 2 sticks of celery and 1 green pepper, diced, to stop the browning, and soften them for 8 minutes, then add 4 cloves of garlic for a minute.

Add 800 g (28 oz) of chopped tomatoes, 120 ml (half a cup) of dry wine and about 720 ml (3 cups) of fish stock, with 2 bay leaves, thyme, a pinch of ground allspice, cayenne and salt. Simmer the gravy for 30 to 45 minutes, until it is thick and the raw tomato taste has gone. Only then lay the fish in, spoon the gravy over, cover and keep it below the boil for 10 to 15 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flakes, about 63°C (145°F) at the thickest part. Shake the pot rather than stir it, so the pieces stay whole. Finish with lemon juice and thin lemon slices, green onion and parsley.

Creole versions, the city's, are rich with tomato and a well-browned roux, the gravy thick enough to coat the fish like a sauce. Cajun versions in the country are often made with catfish or redfish and less roux, or none, so the gravy is lighter and leans on the tomato, the onion and the fish's own juices. Both go over rice. Among its neighbours, a courtbouillon is gentler than a sauce piquante, made for fish rather than game, and redder and looser than an étouffée.

Courtbouillon is old in New Orleans print. Lafcadio Hearn's La Cuisine Créole of 1885 lists a courtbouillon among its recipes, and The Picayune's Creole Cook Book prints a Courtbouillon à la Créole, for which, it says, Creole cooks favour redfish or red snapper over other fish. Where its tomato came from, perhaps Spanish cooking, the evidence is too thin to say.

Fish in shreds means it was stirred or boiled: lay it in last, shake the pot and keep the gravy below the boil. Dry, chalky fish went in too early or cooked too long; it needs only 10 to 15 minutes. A thin, watery gravy was not reduced before the fish went in, and the fish adds water of its own, so simmer the gravy a little thicker than you want. A sharp, raw tomato taste means the gravy was rushed. A muddy, bitter gravy comes from a roux taken too dark or scorched, which buries a fish as delicate as redfish.

Courtbouillon is not on our printed menus. If a guest asks, describe it as redfish simmered in a thick tomato and roux gravy with the trinity, over rice, and say it the Louisiana way, coo-bee-YON. A guest who knows the French word may expect a poaching broth; explain that here it names this saucy fish stew. Whole fish and bone-in steaks carry bones, so say so, and send questions about fish, flour or wine in any dish to the kitchen.

entries.title: Sauce piquante
entries.summary: A Cajun stew rather than a sauce: meat, game or seafood simmered long in a dark roux gravy with the trinity, tomato and plenty of cayenne and hot pepper, served over rice. Piquante means sharp, and the heat is the point.
entries.guest: Sauce piquante is a spicy Cajun stew: a dark roux and tomato gravy with onion, celery and pepper, simmered with chicken, game or alligator and served over rice.

paras: In Cajun country, sauce piquante is not a sauce to pour but a stew to eat: a dark roux, the trinity, tomato and a generous load of cayenne and hot pepper, simmered for hours with whatever the hunt, the swamp or the yard has given. Rabbit, squirrel, venison, duck, turtle, alligator and chicken all go in, shrimp too, and it is always served over rice. Piquante is French for sharp or pricking: the bite of the pepper, and in some pots a splash of vinegar.

It teaches a cook what a dark roux and long simmering do together. The roux gives a deep, roasted flavour, the tomato cooks down into a rich, brick-red gravy, and tough meat that would be chewy in a quick sauce turns tender in two hours.

For about eight: season 1.8 kg (4 lb) of rabbit, chicken thigh or alligator in pieces with salt and cayenne, brown it in oil in a heavy pot, and lift it out. Make a dark roux in the same pot with 115 g (4 oz) each of oil and flour, stirring without stopping until it reaches dark chocolate, 40 minutes or more over a medium flame. Tip in 2 onions, 2 sticks of celery and 2 green peppers, diced, to stop the browning, soften them for 10 minutes, then add 4 cloves of garlic.

Add 800 g (28 oz) of crushed tomatoes, a spoonful of tomato paste, about 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock, bay, thyme, cayenne and hot pepper sauce or chopped fresh hot peppers. Return the meat and simmer, partly covered, stirring now and then so nothing catches: about 1 hour for chicken or alligator tail, by which time chicken is well past 74°C (165°F); 1.5 to 2.5 hours for rabbit, venison or alligator body meat, until the meat is tender and the oil rises in red beads on the surface. Skim some of it off.

Shrimp go in for the last 3 to 5 minutes only. Taste, add a splash of vinegar if the pot wants sharpness, and finish with green onion and parsley. Build the heat in stages. Pepper concentrates as the gravy reduces, so a pot seasoned fiercely at the start can end too hot to enjoy.

Know it against its neighbours. The Creole sauce of the city is a bright tomato sauce on softened trinity, sometimes a light roux, mild enough for eggs and shrimp. Sauce piquante takes a much darker roux, far more heat and long cooking with meat, so it is a stew rather than a sauce. Against a courtbouillon it is the darker, hotter pot, made for game rather than delicate fish.

The French sauce piquante shares only the name. In the classical kitchen it is a brown sauce: white wine and vinegar reduced with shallots, finished with demi-glace, a brown stock sauce reduced until it is glossy and rich, then chopped gherkins and herbs. It belongs to the brown family; the Cajun pot is another thing altogether.

Black flecks in the roux mean it scorched: throw it out and start again, because burnt flour is bitter and stirring cannot hide it. Tough meat has not simmered long enough; keep going until it gives. A burnt bottom comes from a thick gravy left unstirred over too much heat. A greasy surface wants skimming. Rubbery shrimp went in too early. A pot that is too fierce was seasoned hard at the start; more tomato and stock calm it a little, but the cure is to season in stages.

Sauce piquante is a gathering dish. Cajun cooks make it in great pots for family gatherings and cook-offs, simmering through the morning and ladling it over rice by lunchtime, and every family argues for its own meat and its own heat. As with gumbo, the rice is never optional.

Sauce piquante is not on our printed menus. If a guest asks, describe it as a spicy Cajun stew of dark roux, tomato and the trinity, with chicken, game or alligator, over rice, and be honest about the heat: it is meant to bite. Held for service, it stays at 57°C (135°F) or above. Questions about spice, shellfish or flour in any dish go to the kitchen.

entries.title: Creole sauce
entries.summary: The New Orleans tomato sauce: onion, celery and green pepper softened in fat with garlic, then tomatoes, stock, bay, thyme and cayenne, simmered thick. It is the backbone of shrimp Creole and of many Creole fish and egg dishes.
entries.guest: Creole sauce is our New Orleans tomato sauce, built on onion, celery and bell pepper with a little cayenne; on the Shrimp & Grits it carries smoky tasso.

paras: Creole sauce is the tomato sauce of New Orleans. It starts with the holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, softened in butter or oil with garlic. Then tomatoes and a little stock go in with bay, thyme and cayenne, and it simmers until it is thick enough to coat a spoon. Some cooks start it on a light roux for body, and some add a pinch of sugar to soften the acid of the tomatoes.

It matters because so much of the city's cooking stands on it. It is the backbone of shrimp Creole, of Creole omelettes and eggs, and of fish baked or poached à la Créole, which simply means in the Creole style. Learn this one sauce and a whole page of the old menus makes sense.

For about 1 litre (about 1 quart): melt 30 g (1 oz) of butter, or warm 30 ml (2 tbsp) of oil, in a heavy pan over a medium heat. Add 1 large onion, 2 sticks of celery and 1 green pepper, diced, about 450 g (1 lb) in all, and sweat them, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and translucent but not brown. Add 3 cloves of garlic for a minute, just until fragrant; garlic burns fast and turns bitter.

Add 800 g (28 oz) of tinned or peeled ripe tomatoes, chopped, and 240 ml (1 cup) of chicken, shrimp or fish stock, with 2 bay leaves, a few sprigs of thyme, salt, black pepper and cayenne, a pinch to 2.5 ml (1/2 tsp) to taste. Simmer it gently, uncovered, for 30 to 45 minutes, stirring now and then, until the raw tomato edge has gone and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a trail. If it tastes sharp, a pinch of sugar or a knob of butter rounds it. Finish with green onion and parsley, and hold it for service at 57°C (135°F) or above.

For a thicker sauce, start with a blond roux: 30 g (1 oz) each of butter and flour, cooked for about 5 minutes before the trinity goes in. For shrimp Creole, slip 675 g (1.5 lb) of peeled shrimp into the simmering sauce for the last 3 to 4 minutes, only until pink and opaque, about 63°C (145°F), and serve it over rice.

Know it against its neighbours. An Italian tomato sauce starts from onion or garlic in olive oil and leans on basil or oregano; Creole sauce has the trinity, so it tastes of green pepper and celery, and it carries cayenne heat. A Cajun gravy, as in a sauce piquante or a brown stew, stands on a dark roux and tastes roasted and brown; Creole sauce is bright, red and tangy, the tomato in front. The French sauce tomate is another sauce again, with its own entry.

Crunchy vegetables in a long-simmered sauce mean the trinity went in raw with the tomatoes: acid slows softening, so they must be sweated soft first. A watery sauce was not reduced, or the shrimp gave up their water; simmer it thicker before the seafood goes in. A sharp, tinny taste comes from underripe tomatoes or a short simmer. Bitterness means browned garlic or a scorched bottom, so keep the heat gentle and stir.

At Brennan's, Creole sauce is on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, a breakfast and lunch entrée: Louisiana shrimp in Creole sauce over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, with fried okra chips. Our sauce carries tasso, the spiced, smoked pork shoulder used a little at a time as a seasoning meat, so it is smoky as well as tangy. entries.title: Creole rémoulade
entries.summary: The New Orleans rémoulade is a cold, spiced sauce led by Creole mustard, with paprika, cayenne, horseradish, lemon, garlic, celery, green onion and parsley. Pinker and hotter than the French one, it is the sauce of shrimp rémoulade.
entries.guest: Creole rémoulade is a cool, tangy New Orleans sauce, often pink with paprika and sharp with Creole mustard. Ours is a chive rémoulade, cool and herby, for dipping the Crawfish Meat Pies.

paras: Rémoulade, said REM-uh-lahd (RUM-uh-lahd is heard in New Orleans), is a cold sauce for seafood and cold dishes. The New Orleans version is pink to brick red, hot and sharp. Creole mustard leads it: a coarse, stone-ground brown mustard with a vinegary bite. Paprika gives the colour, cayenne the heat, prepared horseradish a nose-clearing sting and lemon the brightness. Garlic, finely chopped celery, green onion and flat-leaf parsley bring crunch and freshness.

It matters because it is one of the sauces that taste of the city. Its great dish is shrimp rémoulade: chilled boiled shrimp dressed in the sauce and set on a bed of shredded iceberg lettuce, the cold, crisp lettuce cooling the heat.

There are two styles. The pink style is built on mayonnaise. For about 500 ml (2 cups) of sauce, start with 240 ml (1 cup) of mayonnaise and stir in 60 ml (4 tbsp) of Creole mustard, 15 ml (1 tbsp) of prepared horseradish, 5 g (2 tsp) of sweet paprika, the juice of half a lemon and one clove of garlic mashed to a paste with a pinch of salt. Add cayenne and hot sauce a pinch and a dash at a time. Fold in about 30 g (4 tbsp) each of finely chopped celery and green onion and about 8 g (2 tbsp) of chopped parsley, then salt to taste.

The red style has no mayonnaise at all. It is a dressing, close to a vinaigrette: Creole mustard, paprika, horseradish, lemon juice or vinegar and the seasonings are whisked together, then oil is whisked in until the mustard holds it in a loose, brick-red emulsion, meaning oil held in tiny droplets through the liquid. Work at about two parts oil to one part mustard, with the acid to taste. Some New Orleans kitchens still make it this way, and it eats hotter and leaner than the pink.

Either way, make it at least an hour ahead and chill it: the flavours marry and the paprika's colour deepens as it rests. Taste it again cold, because cold dulls salt and heat. Keep it covered at 5°C (41°F) or below, as you would any mayonnaise sauce, and dress the shrimp close to service so the lettuce stays crisp.

The French rémoulade, which has its own entry, is white: mayonnaise with mustard, chopped gherkins, capers, herbs and, in Escoffier, a little anchovy essence, close to a tartar sauce. The New Orleans sauce kept the name and went its own way: pinker from paprika, hotter from cayenne and horseradish, and led by mustard rather than by mayonnaise and pickles. Its close New Orleans cousin is ravigote, another cold, sharp sauce for crab and shrimp.

A flat, dull rémoulade lacks acid or salt, or was seasoned warm; add lemon and salt and taste it cold. A thin, weeping one was made with wet shrimp or celery, or is a red dressing whose emulsion has let go; dry everything well and whisk the dressing again with a spoonful of mustard. A harsh, bitter edge comes from old, dusty paprika or too much raw garlic, which sharpens as the sauce rests; use fresh paprika, mash the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt and keep to one clove. A sauce too hot to taste anything else had its cayenne added in one go, so build the heat in pinches.

At Brennan's the sauce appears as a chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard: cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry. The menu does not print the recipe, so whether it is the pink or the red style, and what goes into it, are questions for the kitchen. Rémoulade is also one of the five New Orleans sauces the courtyard turtles are named for, beside Ravigote, Bordelaise, Mignonette and Cocktail.

Describe the New Orleans sauce plainly: cool and tangy, pink with paprika, sharp with Creole mustard and horseradish. Warn a guest who expects the mild French or tartar-style sauce that the Creole one usually has heat. For the chive rémoulade on the meat pies, say cool, tangy and herby, and send questions about egg, mustard, heat or anything else in it to the kitchen, because the house recipe is not printed.

entries.title: Ravigote, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Ravigote is a sharp, herb-led sauce whose name means revived. In France it is a cold vinaigrette with capers, shallot and fines herbes, or a warm velouté sauce; in New Orleans it is lump crab in a cold, creamy dressing.
entries.guest: Ravigote means revived: a sharp sauce of capers, vinegar and herbs. In New Orleans it usually means lump crab in a cold, creamy dressing, sometimes baked hot.

paras: Ravigote, said rah-vee-GOHT, comes from the French verb ravigoter, to revive or perk up, and the sauce does what its name says: it wakes up a plain or rich food with acid, shallot and a handful of fresh herbs. It is not one recipe but three, and the menu line tells you which is meant.

The French kitchen has a cold ravigote, a vinaigrette for calf's head and cold meats, and a warm ravigote built on velouté. New Orleans has a third of its own: crabmeat ravigote, lump crab in a cold, mayonnaise-based dressing. All three share a sharp, acid edge and fresh herbs, and very little else; capers belong to the cold ones.

The cold French ravigote is a seasoned vinaigrette. Escoffier gives it among his cold sauces as an oil and vinegar dressing with small capers, finely chopped onion and the fines herbes, served with calf's head and calf's feet. Work at about three parts oil to one part wine vinegar. For 250 ml (about 1 cup) of sauce, whisk 60 ml (1/4 cup) of vinegar with salt and pepper, then whisk in 180 ml (3/4 cup) of oil.

Fold in about 10 g (1 tbsp) of small capers, rinsed and chopped, 15 ml (1 tbsp) of very finely chopped shallot or onion, and about 8 g (2 tbsp) of fines herbes: chervil, tarragon, chives and flat-leaf parsley, cut fine with a sharp knife so they stay green. Add the herbs within the hour of service, because vinegar dulls their colour as it sits. Spoon it over warm tête de veau, calf's head simmered and rolled, or over cold boiled beef, tongue or poached fish.

The warm ravigote is a different sauce again: a velouté, a stock sauce thickened with a pale roux, sharpened with wine and vinegar. It is taught under the velouté family and named here only so it is not mistaken for the cold ones.

New Orleans took the name and made it a crab dish. Crabmeat ravigote is lump blue crab folded into a cold dressing of mayonnaise sharpened with Creole mustard, capers, green onion, parsley and lemon. Mayonnaise has no place in the French ravigote; here it is the base. A working ratio is about 120 ml (1/2 cup) of dressing to 450 g (1 lb) of lump crab: enough to coat, never to drown.

It is served cold, mounded on lettuce, in a halved avocado or with toast points, as a starter in the city's old-line dining rooms. Some kitchens bake it: crab and dressing go into a ramekin or a cleaned crab shell under breadcrumbs and are heated until the edges bubble. Fold with a spatula, never stir, because lump crab is paid for by the size of its pieces. Keep the crab and the dressing at 5°C (41°F) or below until they are plated.

The faults follow the base. A cold French ravigote turns grey-green and flat when the herbs sit too long in the vinegar, and it separates into oil and vinegar if it is not whisked again before it is spooned. The crab ravigote fails when stirring breaks the lumps into shreds, when crab liquor makes the dressing weep, or when it is overdressed and tastes of mayonnaise rather than crab. A baked ravigote left too long turns oily as the mayonnaise breaks; take it out when the edges bubble.

Both French sauces are classical: Escoffier's A Guide to Modern Cookery, the 1907 English edition of his Guide Culinaire, gives a warm ravigote among the small sauces and a cold one, also called vinaigrette, among the cold sauces. The crab version came later, in the New Orleans restaurants, where mayonnaise, Creole mustard and Gulf crab made a French dressing local.

Which ravigote is on the plate? Read the menu line. Crabmeat ravigote is cold, creamy crab, sharp with mustard and capers, unless the menu says baked or the kitchen has said otherwise at lineup. On a French menu, calf's head or cold meats sauced ravigote come with the sharp herb vinaigrette; when it is the warm velouté, the kitchen will say so at lineup.

At Brennan's the word has a second life: Ravigote is one of the ten courtyard turtles, one of the five named for New Orleans sauces. Questions about shellfish, egg or mustard in any ravigote go to the kitchen.

entries.title: New Orleans barbecue shrimp
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans barbecue shrimp.
entries.summary: New Orleans barbecue shrimp are never barbecued: head-on shrimp cooked in a peppery pan sauce of butter, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon. Credited to Pascal's Manale, the dish is eaten with the hands, a bib and plenty of bread.
entries.guest: Barbecue shrimp in New Orleans means no smoke and no tomato: shrimp cooked in butter with black pepper, garlic and lemon. Our Louisiana Oysters come in that sauce at breakfast and lunch.

paras: New Orleans barbecue shrimp is the city's quiet joke on visitors: nothing is barbecued, smoked or grilled, and there is no tomato. Large head-on Gulf shrimp are cooked in a pan sauce of butter, a heavy hand of black pepper, Worcestershire sauce, garlic and lemon, often with Creole seasoning, and some cooks add rosemary or hot sauce. The result is buttery, peppery and a deep reddish brown.

It matters because the word confuses guests every night. Anyone from outside Louisiana hears barbecue and expects smoke or a sweet red sauce. The server's first job is to say what it is before the plate lands.

The heads carry much of the flavour: the fat inside them melts into the butter and makes the sauce richer and deeper. For 450 g (1 lb) of large head-on shrimp, shells on, have ready 115 g (4 oz) of cold butter cut in cubes, 30 ml (2 tbsp) of Worcestershire, about 30 ml (2 tbsp) of lemon juice, three cloves of garlic, chopped, and 7 to 14 g (1 to 2 tbsp) of coarsely cracked black pepper.

Melt a knob of the butter in a wide pan over medium-high heat, add the garlic for a few seconds, then the shrimp in one layer. Add the Worcestershire, lemon, pepper and seasoning with a splash of shrimp stock or water, and turn the shrimp as they colour. Take them to nearly done, 2 to 4 minutes, the shells pink and the flesh turning opaque; they finish in the sauce, and seafood is cooked to 63°C (145°F). Do not crowd the pan, or the shrimp stew in their own water.

Then lower the heat and swirl in the cold butter a few cubes at a time, shaking the pan, until the liquid turns glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon; with a full pan or a slow hand, lift the shrimp into a warm bowl before the butter goes in, and pour the sauce over them. That is a pan emulsion: butter held in a little liquid, the idea behind a beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, the French butter sauce. Once the butter is in it must not boil, and it must not sit on the pass, the counter where finished plates wait for a server, or it splits into a pool of grease.

A greasy, split sauce boiled after the butter went in, or waited too long; off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of hot stock or water, and next time serve it straight away. Tight, rubbery shrimp were overcooked or left in the hot sauce; pull them when just opaque. Soft, mushy flesh means head-on shrimp were kept too long before cooking, because enzymes in the head soften the tail. A thin, pale sauce had too much liquid when the butter went in; reduce it first. A flat taste wants more pepper or more lemon: the dish is meant to be peppery, and the lemon keeps the butter from cloying.

The dish is credited to Pascal's Manale, an Uptown restaurant on Napoleon Avenue. By the family's account, in 1954, though some tellings say 1953, a regular described a buttery, peppery shrimp dish he had eaten in Chicago, and the kitchen worked out its own version, which he liked better. Tell it as their story; why it took the name barbecue has never been settled.

This is a dish eaten with the hands. Bring a bib, extra napkins, a bowl for shells and plenty of hot French bread, because the sauce is the point and the bread is how a guest eats it. Show a guest new to head-on shrimp how to twist off the head, peel the tail and, if they like, suck the head for its juices. Describe it as buttery and peppery, rich rather than hot.

Brennan's uses the name on two plates. The Louisiana Oysters, a breakfast and lunch starter, are oysters in the buttery, peppery sauce with pickled collard greens, shallots and a fried saltine crumble; how they are cooked and plated is confirmed at lineup. The Louisiana BBQ Lobster, the second course of the dinner tasting, gives lobster the same treatment over a white bean stew with ’nduja, en-DOO-yah, a soft, spicy pork sausage from Calabria. The house recipe is not published, so describe it as a buttery, peppery New Orleans BBQ sauce, and send questions about the Worcestershire, traditionally made with anchovy, or anything else in it to the kitchen.

entries.title: Blackening
entries.summary: Blackening is Paul Prudhomme's method: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend and seared in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking, so the spices toast to a dark crust while the inside stays moist.
entries.guest: Blackened means coated in a spice blend and seared in a very hot iron pan: a dark, spiced crust outside, moist inside. It is blackened, never burnt.

paras: Blackening is a young technique, created by the chef Paul Prudhomme at K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen in the French Quarter around 1980. A fish fillet, classically redfish, is dipped in melted butter, coated thickly in a paprika-led spice blend and laid in a cast-iron pan heated dry until it is past smoking. In a couple of minutes a side the butter and spices toast into a dark, almost black crust while the fish inside stays moist.
Blackened is not burnt: burnt is bitter and acrid, blackened is toasty, spiced and savoury, and the difference is heat and speed.

Choose fillets of even thickness, about 1.25 cm (1/2 inch), so the inside cooks through in the time the crust takes to form; a thick fillet burns outside before it is done. Heat a heavy cast-iron pan dry over the highest flame for about 10 minutes, until it smokes hard and the surface is well above 260°C (500°F). No oil goes into the pan: the butter on the fish is the only fat.

Dip each fillet in melted butter, then press the spice blend onto both sides in an even, generous coat. Lay it in the pan away from you. Cook about 2 minutes, until the underside is dark and crusted, turn it once, spoon a little melted butter over the top and cook 1 to 2 minutes more. Fish is done at 63°C (145°F), when it flakes at the thickest part. Serve at once, crust up.

The blend is led by paprika. A common working proportion, by volume, is 3 parts sweet paprika and 2 to 2.5 parts salt to 1 part each of onion powder, garlic powder and cayenne, three-quarters of a part each of white and black pepper, and half a part each of dried thyme and oregano. Paprika gives the colour and toasts to the dark crust; cayenne and the peppers give heat; the herbs give a savoury, almost smoky note. Sugar has no place in it: sugar burns before the fish is cooked.

Blackening makes a great deal of smoke, and that is the method working: butter and spices meeting iron above 260°C (500°F). Restaurants do it under a strong extraction hood; at home it is best done outdoors on a burner, which is why home kitchens fill with smoke and set off alarms. Keep a lid beside the pan, never throw water on burning butter, and handle the iron with a dry cloth: it stays fiercely hot long after the flame is off.

A bitter, burnt crust means the fish stayed on too long, often because it was cut too thick, or the last batch's burnt residue was left in the pan. A grey, soggy coating comes from a cool or crowded pan. Fish that sticks and tears was turned too early; fish raw at the centre was cut too thick.

Blackened redfish became a national craze in the 1980s. That demand, with heavy commercial netting, drove red drum, the redfish, down hard. By the late 1980s federal waters of the Gulf were closed to red drum harvest, and Louisiana had closed its own commercial fishery; red drum is now a game fish there, for anglers rather than the market. Redfish on a menu today is farmed or legally caught elsewhere, and cooks blacken drum, catfish, chicken and vegetables too.

At Brennan's the method goes on tofu. The Blackened Tofu, a dinner entrée, is Tien Dat tofu, made fresh across the river by a local Vietnamese maker, blackened to a dark, spiced crust and set over Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. Because the classic method uses butter, and the rice grits may be cooked with stock, the house asks every server to check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

Describe blackened food as a dark, spiced crust from a very hot iron pan, moist inside, warm with spice rather than fiery. Tell a guest who fears burnt food that the dark colour is toasted paprika and herbs. The Blackened Tofu runs to moderate spice; a guest wary of heat should hear that, and the kitchen can say more. Blackened is a method, not a sauce.

entries.title: Grillades and grits
entries.summary: Thin pieces of veal or beef round, pounded, seasoned, browned hard and braised in a brown roux gravy with the trinity and tomato until fork tender, then spooned over slow-cooked grits. A Creole brunch classic with country roots.
entries.guest: Grillades are thin slices of beef or veal braised slowly in a dark gravy with onion, pepper and tomato, spooned over creamy grits: old New Orleans brunch food.

paras: Grillades, said gree-YAHDS, are thin pieces of veal or beef round, pounded flat, seasoned, browned hard and braised slowly in a brown roux gravy with the trinity and tomato until fork tender. Spooned over grits they become grillades and grits, a Creole brunch classic that suits a crowd, since the gravy improves overnight.

The name comes from the French griller, to grill, yet nothing here is grilled: the meat is seared, then stewed. Veal is the old city choice, beef round the everyday one and pork the country one; the round is lean and hard-working, which is why it wants pounding.

Cut 900 g (2 lb) of top round or veal round across the grain into slices 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick, pound them to about 5 mm (1/4 inch) and cut palm-sized pieces. Season with salt, black pepper and cayenne, dust with flour and brown in hot oil, a few at a time, 1 to 2 minutes a side. The browned bits left behind, the fond, flavour the gravy.

In the same pot cook 60 g (2 oz) of flour in 60 ml (1/4 cup) of oil over medium-low heat to a medium brown roux, the colour of milk chocolate, 25 to 35 minutes. Add 300 g (10 oz) of diced trinity, which stops the roux darkening, and soften it for 5 to 8 minutes, adding garlic at the end. Stir in 400 g (14 oz) of chopped tomatoes, 750 ml (about 3 cups) of beef or veal stock, thyme, two bay leaves and 30 to 60 ml (2 to 4 tbsp) of red wine or red wine vinegar to cut the richness.

Return the meat, cover and braise at a bare simmer or in a 160°C (320°F) oven for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, until fork tender. Season once the gravy has reduced and finish with green onion and parsley. To hold, keep the meat covered under its gravy at 57°C (135°F) or above, the FDA Food Code's hot-holding line; meat left out dries and turns stringy.
The gravy takes about 60 g (2 oz) of flour, cooked in the same weight of fat, for every 1 litre (about 1 quart) of liquid: a generous hand, because a brown roux thickens less than a pale one.

Grits take 1 part to 4 parts liquid by volume: 160 g (1 cup) to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of water, or milk and water, with 5 g (1 tsp) of salt, whisked in a thin stream. Stone-ground grits, coarse and carrying the germ, may need more liquid and 45 to 60 minutes of low heat, stirred often; quick grits, ground finer, take about 5 minutes. Finish with butter, and for cheese grits stir in 115 g (4 oz) of grated sharp cheddar off the heat.

Most faults come from hurry. A crowded pot steams the meat grey, a hard boil makes it stringy and a roux pulled too soon leaves the gravy pale and floury. Grits lump when poured in fast and stiffen on the hold; loosen them with hot milk.

The usual telling puts the roots at the boucherie, the communal pig killing of the south Louisiana countryside, where fresh pork was cut thin and fried with onions over the fire. It is a likely story, not a documented one. What is certain is that the city took it up as a breakfast and brunch dish.

There are no grillades on the Brennan's menus we study, but each half has a cousin. The Cheddar Grits, a breakfast and lunch side, are the cheese grits variation. The Eggs Owen shares the idea of beef slow-cooked in a rich gravy for the morning, but it is short rib débris, DAY-bree, beef braised in red wine until it falls into shreds in its deep, winey gravy.

Call grillades what they are: thin slices of beef or veal braised in a dark gravy with onion, pepper and tomato, over creamy grits. A guest who hears grill expects a steak, so say soft, rich and gently spiced. At Brennan's breakfast and lunch, steer a guest who wants grillades to the Eggs Owen. Questions about flour, dairy or anything else go to the service note and the kitchen.
